medical.title: Testing BRCA1 variants reveals differences in breast cancer risk
medical.summary: Researchers at the Francis Crick Institute have tested thousands of possible BRCA1 mutations in mammary gland cells to shed light on which genetic variants confer a high risk of developing breast cancer. Research like this holds potential to improve how genetic results are interpreted in the future.

medical.title: Clinical trial explores potential brain health benefits of dietary supplement
medical.summary: A dietary supplement called urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity in middle-aged adults with obesity, according to a University of Oklahoma study published in JAMA Network Open. The findings could help researchers better understand the relationship between the supplement, blood vessel function and brain health.

medical.title: AI-powered imaging tracks thousands of brain cancer cells moving through living tissue
medical.summary: By combining live imaging of brain tissue with artificial intelligence, researchers at Uppsala University have developed a method that reveals how individual glioblastoma cells spread through the brain, how they can switch between different ways of moving and how they are affected by cancer treatments. An increased understanding of tumor cell invasion might in the long term contribute to more effective therapies.

medical.title: Team develops Asia's first AI-powered platform for one-stop autism support
medical.summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects approximately 1 in every 100 children worldwide, yet many families face lengthy waits for professional assessment and intervention services, often missing the critical window for early support. To address this challenge, researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have developed "ASD Super Agent," Asia's first integrated AI platform for autism support.

medical.title: Declining hippocampal connectivity may predict worsening symptoms in young people at risk for psychosis
medical.summary: One of the central problems in psychiatry is the lack of objective biomarkers: While other areas of medicine have reliable methods for diagnosis and treatment, like X-rays or blood tests, psychiatrists and researchers rely on the patient's self-reported symptoms. In a new study, researchers identified connectivity within the hippocampus as a novel biomarker candidate for the early risk stages of psychotic disorders—and a potential predictor for difficult-to-treat negative symptoms.

medical.title: New clinical definition of obesity could help target care more effectively, saving time and money
medical.summary: The traditional way of assessing whether someone is overweight using body mass index (BMI) may fail to capture whether excess body fat is harmful and could be supplemented with a second measure when assessing patients, a new UCL study suggests.

medical.title: Little-known protein offers a potential target for treating Chagas disease
medical.summary: In Brazil, researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) and their collaborators have identified a promising target for developing new Chagas disease treatments. In laboratory tests, the group succeeded in interrupting the infection cycle of the Trypanosoma cruzi parasite by reducing the production of one of its proteins.

medical.title: We cannot predict the development of social anxiety from brain scans, study says
medical.summary: Freezing when a stranger enters the room, retreating to a parent's lap or being reluctant to approach other children: inhibited behavior in childhood is strongly associated with social anxiety disorder later in life. But is this inhibition also reflected in the brain, and could brain scans therefore help identify the early signs of social anxiety disorder?

medical.title: Low-cost parenting app reduces sexual violence against adolescent girls by more than half, study finds
medical.summary: A digital parenting program has reduced sexual violence and exploitation among adolescent girls in Tanzania by more than half, according to new research led by the University of Oxford's Department of Social Policy and Intervention. A separate study suggests the program could also deliver substantial savings to health services, offering a potentially affordable way to prevent violence against children.

medical.title: What families should know about postpartum psychosis
medical.summary: It's no wonder most people hadn't heard much about postpartum psychosis until it entered the news ecosystem in tragic fashion this year with the Lindsay Clancy case. Despite its severity, the illness isn't recognized as a standalone category in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)—the guidebook published by the American Psychiatric Association for classifying everything from anxiety and depression to obsessive-compulsive and trauma-related disorders.

medical.title: Urgent care emerges as a promising setting for imaging low back pain
medical.summary: Low back pain accounts for some of the highest health care spending in the U.S. Given how many patients are affected, even small changes in imaging practices could substantially impact health care resource use. A retrospective cohort study led by Mass General Brigham researchers found that only 24 of 2,924 urgent care lumbar spine X-rays for uncomplicated low back pain were followed by emergency department advanced imaging within 30 days.

medical.title: Psychedelic aftereffects may offer a window into psychotic symptoms
medical.summary: Every night, as he fell asleep, a 25-year-old man saw an eye in his ceiling. It was huge and unblinking, and it felt as if the whole world was being sucked into it. He didn't have psychosis, and he wasn't on drugs. But he had taken psychedelics in the past, and he was worried enough to contact Max Greenwald, an M.D.-Ph.D. student at Yale School of Medicine, with a question: Was he developing psychosis?

medical.title: Team discovers key pathway in heart lymphatic vessel development
medical.summary: Researchers at Children's Hospital Los Angeles have uncovered molecular signals that shape a little-understood network of vessels in the heart, offering new insight into both its normal formation and its response to injury.

medical.title: Jolting awake often associated with poorer sleep and higher anxiety, survey finds
medical.summary: People who frequently startle awake while falling asleep—a phenomenon researchers call "sleep starts" or hypnic jerks—report poorer sleep quality, greater insomnia severity and higher anxiety than those who do not, according to a new study published in PLOS Mental Health by Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus of Paris Lodron University Salzburg, Austria, and colleagues.

medical.title: Children's recess activity in extreme heat highlights need for adult-guided safety measures
medical.summary: In a survey of 170 elementary students in the Phoenix, Arizona, metropolitan area over August–September 2024 (the average maximum temperature during this period was 97°F; 36.1°C), students reported feeling "a lot hot" directly after recess in 45% of surveys—and higher perceived heat was associated with greater physical activity intensity, according to a study published in PLOS Global Public Health by Kylie Wilson from the University of Arizona Cancer Center, United States, and colleagues.

medical.title: Could your genes affect your medications? New study highlights high probability
medical.summary: Everyone in a diverse, nearly 100,000-person sample carried at least one genetic variant that affects how their body processes medications, and a quarter of those people had been prescribed a medication that is known to be impacted by the variant they carried, a new University of Pittsburgh–led analysis reveals in Science Translational Medicine.

medical.title: How gut antibodies protect against colon cancer
medical.summary: Antibodies that coat the lining of your gut may be playing an important role in preventing colon cancer from developing, Rockefeller University scientists have discovered.

medical.title: Giving the voice a face: Virtual avatars may ease distress in schizophrenia
medical.summary: Patients with schizophrenia can come face to face in virtual reality with an avatar representing the voice they hear, which is often threatening or abusive. According to a study by researchers at Semmelweis University, published in Acta Psychologica, the treatment was associated with significant reductions in the frequency of the voices and the distress they caused, with more than 40% of participants showing meaningful improvement overall. While the results are promising, the researchers stress that VR-Avatar therapy cannot replace medication and should only be used as an add-on treatment.

medical.title: Training AI to see cells in context improves detection in pathology images
medical.summary: Artificial intelligence can help identify cells in digital pathology images, but densely packed tissue remains a challenge: neighboring cells may be merged, counted twice or missed entirely. Researchers at Koç University have developed a training strategy that improves detection by teaching AI to consider how cells are arranged within the tissue.

medical.title: Youth and caregiver reports of mental health issues differ, but both perspectives needed
medical.summary: Psychiatric assessments of children and adolescents commonly incorporate reports from both youth and their caregivers. However, they may identify substantially different mental health problems, potentially influencing diagnosis, treatment planning and estimates of psychiatric disorder prevalence.

medical.title: Family activities, volunteering and exercise show links to greater psychological resilience, study finds
medical.summary: A research team led by the School of Public Health, LKS Faculty of Medicine of the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), recently conducted one of the largest and most systematic studies to date on predictors of psychological resilience. Analyzing data from 26,210 Hong Kong residents, the researchers systematically evaluated 208 candidate predictors and ultimately identified 35 factors associated with an individual's capacity to cope with adversity.

medical.title: New 'FITdb' database reveals the genetic drivers of immune cell function
medical.summary: Scientists at La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) have developed a critical hub for functional genomics and immune cell research. LJI Assistant Professor Miguel Reina-Campos directs the new Functional Immunogenomics and Transcriptomics database (FITdb), a freely accessible resource that brings together functional genomics datasets for immune cell investigations.

medical.title: New review of the first oral PCSK9 drug, a needle-free option for high cholesterol
medical.summary: A new review from Binghamton University School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Science explores how Lipfendra (enlicitide) can be beneficial for those who have intolerances to injectable medications. The review was recently published in Annals of Pharmacotherapy and was authored by clinical assistant professors Taylor Clark, Rachel Lucas and Mia Lussier, as well as assistant professor Azadeh Nasuhidehnavi.

medical.title: For your health—the large and growing benefits of being smoke-free
medical.summary: It's important to celebrate big accomplishments. And when it comes to our health, the drop in U.S. smoking rates over the last six decades is certainly one to cheer.

medical.title: Drug ads can influence AI treatment recommendations, study finds
medical.summary: As people increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for health information, a new study by researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai raises questions about what happens when commercial advertising appears alongside a clinical question. The findings were reported in the Nov. 11 online issue of The Lancet Digital Health.

science.title: Superconducting vortices provide experimental evidence that clogging is a phase transition
science.summary: Clogging is a phenomenon in which moving particles get stuck, slowing or blocking the flow, but how this transition occurs has remained experimentally unproven. Researchers from Science Tokyo studied superconducting vortices to demonstrate that clogging is a nonequilibrium phase transition. Using a two-step measurement protocol, they distinguished clogging from conventional pinning and revealed that both transitions share a critical point, offering new insights into predicting and controlling clogging across diverse systems.

science.title: Looping DNA may help flowers grow nectar-producing organs
science.summary: Nectaries are specialized floral tissues that secrete nectar to attract pollinators. Although the protein CRABS CLAW (CRC) is established as essential for nectary formation, the exact molecular mechanisms governing how it drives organ growth and secretion have remained unknown.

science.title: What is science? Even scientists can't agree
science.summary: Scientists spend their careers trying to understand the world, but a new study suggests they have surprisingly different ideas about what science itself is. The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science even more than the general public does. Of the 18 descriptions of science examined, few received unqualified endorsement from scientists, who often expressed reservations even about ideas they generally agreed with.

science.title: Asteroid mining will crash the platinum market, but that's good news for Earth
science.summary: Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question—what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

science.title: A lingering blue glow and unexpected energy levels hint at new ways to control light in advanced materials
science.summary: Scientists from the Physics Department and Organic Electroactive Materials research group at Durham University have made significant advances in understanding how materials absorb and release light in two recently published research papers in Nature Communications.

science.title: Scientists find some of the 'very last wild and healthy ecosystems' in the world's oceans untouched by humans
science.summary: Humans have left their mark on virtually every place on the planet, from the deep sea to the peaks of the highest mountains. But a few very remote atolls in the Pacific Ocean may be exceptions. A new Frontiers in Marine Science study has found two coral atolls, Bikar and Bokak, located on the territory of the Marshall Islands, to be some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region and perhaps the world.

science.title: Living with humility took on social weight in the late Middle Ages, historian argues
science.summary: We're deep in the Middle Ages. In the mind's eye, monks stagger past, flagellating themselves to cleanse their sins and demonstrate their humility before God and creation. This was a time when humility—humilitas—was considered one of the fundamental virtues of Christian life.

science.title: How pipes became status symbols in 18th-century Sweden
science.summary: In the 18th century, a clay tobacco pipe could reveal more than you might think. Its length, quality and condition, as well as the way it was used, could signal social status. In a new doctoral thesis, Lund University archaeologist Robert Bergman Carter shows how smokeways at the time served as clear markers of status.

science.title: Why holding on to loyal donors is not the right advice for every nonprofit
science.summary: As humanitarian funding shrinks, conventional fundraising wisdom says to hold on to loyal donors. But new research shows that the value of a donor depends on how a nonprofit is set up. For many organizations, winning new donors matters more than keeping loyal ones.

science.title: Deep-sea mollusk houses bacteria in tiny 'dragon balls,' revealing a new symbiotic structure
science.summary: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have discovered a previously unknown specialized organelle structure in a deep-sea mollusk living at cold seeps in the South China Sea. Dedicated to maintaining bacterial symbiosis, this newly identified survival mechanism provides new insights into how deep-sea organisms adapt to nearly oxygen-free environments and opens new directions for research on chemosymbiosis, organelle evolution and deep-sea ecosystems.

science.title: New method maps DNA folding and epigenetic marks in single cells
science.summary: A new experimental procedure developed by researchers at Yale School of Medicine could help scientists better understand how DNA structure influences disease and development.

science.title: When rain finally does come to drylands, only some microbes in the soil 'awaken'
science.summary: In arid regions, the microbes that power threatened dryland soil ecosystems called biological soil crusts stay dormant over long periods, only "awakening" when they sense moisture from infrequent rainfall. Now, a team led by researchers at Penn State—driven by projections that those biocrusts will decline by as much as 40% in the next 45 years—found that when a dryland soil does get wet, most of the microbes in the biocrust stay inactive. It's a discovery that will inform ongoing efforts to conserve and restore biocrusts, according to the researchers.

science.title: Biologists reveal chlorophyll-building enzyme's structure for first time and clarify its mechanism
science.summary: Plants are green because of a pigment that is key to photosynthesis: chlorophyll. In its production, the enzyme chlorophyll synthase plays an important role. As part of an international collaboration, researchers from Osnabrück University, the Center Algatech in Třeboň and the University of Sheffield have now succeeded in deciphering the structure of this enzyme and gaining valuable insights into its mechanism. The findings are published in the journal Nature Chemical Biology.

science.title: Scientists challenge the dream of bringing extinct species back to life
science.summary: Could extinction itself become a thing of the past? Advances in biotechnology, including ancient DNA sequencing, genome analysis and gene editing, have led some to believe that it may be possible to bring extinct species back to life.

science.title: Chip identifies cells by their electrical signature, then separates them with a precisely aimed sound wave
science.summary: In biomedicine, sorting cells accurately without damaging them remains a persistent problem. Current methods, like fluorescence-activated cell sorting, rely on labeling the cells extrinsically, which can stress the cells, alter their behavior and even interfere with the assay. A collaborative study between researchers in Singapore and China has now developed a noninvasive, label-free method to sort cells.

science.title: From remedy to prevention: Researchers call for proactive approach to protect the human right to water
science.summary: More than 2 billion people, or approximately one-quarter of the world's population, lack access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene, according to the United Nations Children's Fund. Today, 16 years after the U.N. General Assembly recognized this access as a fundamental human right, its legal protection is well established, but the reality on the ground lags behind.

science.title: Symbolic clay figurines change our understanding of the prehistoric Middle East
science.summary: Newly discovered artifacts are evidence of the earliest known example of a tradition of making clay figurines in the Middle East—and challenge long-held beliefs about when and how clay began to be used for symbolic purposes in the region, according to a study published in PLOS One by Laurent Davin from The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel, and colleagues.

science.title: Monkey foot and palm prints differ between individuals, as they do in humans
science.summary: In three species of monkey, the complex pattern of ridges on the feet and palms varies between individuals, similar to human fingerprints, according to a study published in the open-access journal PLOS One by Juliana Vieira Flores Sales at Universidade de Brasília and colleagues.

science.title: Misunderstandings about statistics common even among experienced researchers
science.summary: Even researchers and people with extensive training in statistics often find it difficult to interpret statistical results correctly. This is shown by a new systematic review carried out by Uppsala University and others, in which researchers have analyzed 55 studies involving over 15,000 participants. The work is published in PLOS One.

science.title: Spain's massive stone tombs reveal collective burials continued well into Bronze Age
science.summary: Iberian people continued using, and possibly building, massive necropolises well into the Bronze Age, according to a study published in PLOS One by Eduardo Vijande-Vila of the University of Cádiz, Spain, and colleagues.

science.title: Excess reliance on AI could harm independent thinking in humanities education
science.summary: The increasing use of content generated using artificial intelligence (AI) tools in university humanities classrooms is challenging what we think of as traditional academic integrity, intellectual responsibility and the authority of teachers, according to research in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development.

science.title: Ancient DNA reveals rare genetic condition behind a 1,600-year-old infant's single eye socket
science.summary: Cyclopia is the most severe form of a rare birth condition in which the developing brain fails to divide into two separate halves. This can also affect facial development, sometimes leaving the baby with a single eye socket in the center of the forehead and severe facial abnormalities. Most babies born with this condition either die before or soon after birth. It is so rare that it occurs in roughly 1 in 100,000 births, so finding physical evidence of it from modern times is difficult, let alone from historical ones.

environment.title: US companies apply to explore deep-sea mining in area bordering Pacific island states
environment.summary: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back. The applications are part of a broader move by U.S. companies to […]

environment.title: What do a bean and a flamingo have in common? Finding the unexpected in nature photos
environment.summary: Photographer Andrew Zuckerman took a moment longer than usual to look closely at a bean that was sprouting in his studio. “There was this one bean that sort of had this incredibly elegant curve, and I thought, ‘God, that’s exactly like the flamingo from like 15 years ago,’” Zuckerman tells Mongabay in a video call. […]

environment.title: Angolan hunters protect Southern Africa’s internationally important wetland
environment.summary: Four years ago, elders from several different communities in Angola’s southeastern highlands approached environmental anthropologist Kerllen Costa, saying they’d noticed an influx of people from outside the highlands coming there to hunt for bushmeat without obtaining permission from local chiefs. Sometimes the outsiders recruited locals to hunt on their behalf. These hunting parties were disregarding […]

environment.title: US brand StarKist suspends tuna sourcing from vessels accused of exploiting Indonesian fishers
environment.summary: U.S. tuna brand StarKist has announced a halt on purchases from fishing vessels linked to forced labor practices in a recent report. It also says it has hired an outside firm to investigate after an Indonesian migrant fishers’ union demanded a binding labor agreement with the company. In a statement sent to Mongabay on Nov. […]

environment.title: Weird and wonderful wildlife revealed in underexplored mountains
environment.summary: A long-term camera trap study has uncovered a treasure trove of wildlife in the Annamite mountains, that run through Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. The mountains have been called the “Amazon of Asia” owing to the huge variety of species here. With hunting and tree loss threatening the area, conservationists are racing to formulate a plan […]

environment.title: Investigation continues in Indonesia after first conviction in 3-ton pangolin trafficking case
environment.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesian investigators say they expect further developments in a major wildlife trafficking case after an intermediary was sentenced to nine years in prison over the discovery of 3.05 metric tons of pangolin scales at the country’s largest port in February this year. “We’re continuing to expand the investigation to dismantle this illegal […]

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

mix_items.summary: Candidatul României la funcţia de Secretar general al Francofoniei, Dacian Cioloş, a anunţat, miercuri, lansarea unui program de cooperare academică între România şi Uniunea Africană, prin care universităţile româneşti vor pune la dispoziţia tinerilor africani până la 1.709 burse de studiu, începând cu anul universitar 2027–2028.

mix_items.summary: Dr. Daniela Ionescu: 7 din 10 copii și 6 din 10 adulți care ajung la cabinet prezintă respirație orală, sforăit sau semne sugestive pentru apnee în somn Respirația pe gură, sforăitul frecvent și somnul agitat pot fi semne ale unor probleme respiratorii care merită investigate, inclusiv apneea obstructivă în somn; Rețeaua de Clinici ORL Dr. […] Articolul Medicii avertizează: respirația pe gură în timpul copilăriei poate ascunde probleme de somn și poate fi asociată cu modificări ale dezvoltării feței și maxilarelor apare prima dată în Romania Pozitiva .

mix_items.summary: București, 11 noiembrie 2026 Rezultatele recente ale evaluărilor internaționale confirmă una dintre cele mai mari provocări ale sistemului educațional românesc: accesul inegal la oportunități de învățare și dificultățile persistente în dezvoltarea competențelor de bază. mix_items.summary: La un an de la lansare, programul „Susținem cele mai grele începuturi” sprijină dotarea a șapte unități medicale, modernizarea a cinci centre de monitorizare a nou-născuților și dezvoltarea unei platforme digitale dedicate monitorizării copiilor. Cinci centre de monitorizare a nou-născuților prematuri și cu risc au fost modernizate și dotate pentru a asigura evaluarea și urmărirea […] Articolul Salvați Copiii România, Mastercard și Banca Transilvania vor contribui la îmbunătățirea îngrijirii medicale pentru peste 4.000 de nou-născuți anual apare prima dată în Romania Pozitiva .

mix_items.summary: O masă caldă după o zi de mers, un loc unde să înnoptezi, o bicicletă reparată sau o experiență care te apropie de oamenii locului. Sunt lucruri simple, dar nu întotdeauna ușor de găsit de-a lungul celor peste 1.600 de kilometri ai Via Transilvanica, primul traseu pedestru de interes național în scop recreativ din România. mix_items.summary: Județul Vaslui intră oficial pe harta turismului de aventură, după inaugurarea primului traseu de via fermentata din lume. Inspirat de… The post Uită de via ferrata! La Vaslui s-a deschis cel mai spectaculos traseu de via fermentata appeared first on Times New Roman .

mix_items.summary: Cotația petrolului european a trecut prin cea mai mare scădere săptămânală de la începutul pandemiei de coronavirus, de -16% săptămâna… The post Vești proaste pentru șoferi! S-a ieftinit petrolul, deci va crește prețul benzinei la pompă appeared first on Times New Roman .

mix_items.summary: “Start în educație” în anul școlar 2026-2027: 5 milioane de euro pentru îmbunătățirea accesului la educație timpurie de calitate pentru... mix_items.summary: Peste 500 de copii au participat la activități de educație nonformală și wellbeing derulate de Fundația Inocenți cu sprijinul Pepco România. The post Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Testing BRCA1 variants reveals differences in breast cancer risk
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Francis Crick Institute have tested thousands of possible BRCA1 mutations in mammary gland cells to shed light on which genetic variants confer a high risk of developing breast cancer. Research like this holds potential to improve how genetic results are interpreted in the future.

mix_items.title: Superconducting vortices provide experimental evidence that clogging is a phase transition
mix_items.summary: Clogging is a phenomenon in which moving particles get stuck, slowing or blocking the flow, but how this transition occurs has remained experimentally unproven. Researchers from Science Tokyo studied superconducting vortices to demonstrate that clogging is a nonequilibrium phase transition. Using a two-step measurement protocol, they distinguished clogging from conventional pinning and revealed that both transitions share a critical point, offering new insights into predicting and controlling clogging across diverse systems.

mix_items.title: Looping DNA may help flowers grow nectar-producing organs
mix_items.summary: Nectaries are specialized floral tissues that secrete nectar to attract pollinators. Although the protein CRABS CLAW (CRC) is established as essential for nectary formation, the exact molecular mechanisms governing how it drives organ growth and secretion have remained unknown.

mix_items.title: Clinical trial explores potential brain health benefits of dietary supplement
mix_items.summary: A dietary supplement called urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity in middle-aged adults with obesity, according to a University of Oklahoma study published in JAMA Network Open. The findings could help researchers better understand the relationship between the supplement, blood vessel function and brain health.

mix_items.title: What is science? Even scientists can't agree
mix_items.summary: Scientists spend their careers trying to understand the world, but a new study suggests they have surprisingly different ideas about what science itself is. The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science even more than the general public does. Of the 18 descriptions of science examined, few received unqualified endorsement from scientists, who often expressed reservations even about ideas they generally agreed with.

mix_items.title: Asteroid mining will crash the platinum market, but that's good news for Earth
mix_items.summary: Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question—what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

mix_items.title: AI-powered imaging tracks thousands of brain cancer cells moving through living tissue
mix_items.summary: By combining live imaging of brain tissue with artificial intelligence, researchers at Uppsala University have developed a method that reveals how individual glioblastoma cells spread through the brain, how they can switch between different ways of moving and how they are affected by cancer treatments. An increased understanding of tumor cell invasion might in the long term contribute to more effective therapies.

mix_items.title: A lingering blue glow and unexpected energy levels hint at new ways to control light in advanced materials
mix_items.summary: Scientists from the Physics Department and Organic Electroactive Materials research group at Durham University have made significant advances in understanding how materials absorb and release light in two recently published research papers in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Scientists find some of the 'very last wild and healthy ecosystems' in the world's oceans untouched by humans
mix_items.summary: Humans have left their mark on virtually every place on the planet, from the deep sea to the peaks of the highest mountains. But a few very remote atolls in the Pacific Ocean may be exceptions. A new Frontiers in Marine Science study has found two coral atolls, Bikar and Bokak, located on the territory of the Marshall Islands, to be some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region and perhaps the world.

mix_items.title: Team develops Asia's first AI-powered platform for one-stop autism support
mix_items.summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects approximately 1 in every 100 children worldwide, yet many families face lengthy waits for professional assessment and intervention services, often missing the critical window for early support. To address this challenge, researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have developed "ASD Super Agent," Asia's first integrated AI platform for autism support.

mix_items.title: Declining hippocampal connectivity may predict worsening symptoms in young people at risk for psychosis
mix_items.summary: One of the central problems in psychiatry is the lack of objective biomarkers: While other areas of medicine have reliable methods for diagnosis and treatment, like X-rays or blood tests, psychiatrists and researchers rely on the patient's self-reported symptoms. In a new study, researchers identified connectivity within the hippocampus as a novel biomarker candidate for the early risk stages of psychotic disorders—and a potential predictor for difficult-to-treat negative symptoms.

mix_items.title: Living with humility took on social weight in the late Middle Ages, historian argues
mix_items.summary: We're deep in the Middle Ages. In the mind's eye, monks stagger past, flagellating themselves to cleanse their sins and demonstrate their humility before God and creation. This was a time when humility—humilitas—was considered one of the fundamental virtues of Christian life.

mix_items.title: New clinical definition of obesity could help target care more effectively, saving time and money
mix_items.summary: The traditional way of assessing whether someone is overweight using body mass index (BMI) may fail to capture whether excess body fat is harmful and could be supplemented with a second measure when assessing patients, a new UCL study suggests.

mix_items.title: Little-known protein offers a potential target for treating Chagas disease
mix_items.summary: In Brazil, researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) and their collaborators have identified a promising target for developing new Chagas disease treatments. In laboratory tests, the group succeeded in interrupting the infection cycle of the Trypanosoma cruzi parasite by reducing the production of one of its proteins.

mix_items.title: We cannot predict the development of social anxiety from brain scans, study says
mix_items.summary: Freezing when a stranger enters the room, retreating to a parent's lap or being reluctant to approach other children: inhibited behavior in childhood is strongly associated with social anxiety disorder later in life. But is this inhibition also reflected in the brain, and could brain scans therefore help identify the early signs of social anxiety disorder?

mix_items.title: How pipes became status symbols in 18th-century Sweden
mix_items.summary: In the 18th century, a clay tobacco pipe could reveal more than you might think. Its length, quality and condition, as well as the way it was used, could signal social status. In a new doctoral thesis, Lund University archaeologist Robert Bergman Carter shows how smokeways at the time served as clear markers of status.

mix_items.title: Why holding on to loyal donors is not the right advice for every nonprofit
mix_items.summary: As humanitarian funding shrinks, conventional fundraising wisdom says to hold on to loyal donors. But new research shows that the value of a donor depends on how a nonprofit is set up. For many organizations, winning new donors matters more than keeping loyal ones.

mix_items.title: Low-cost parenting app reduces sexual violence against adolescent girls by more than half, study finds
mix_items.summary: A digital parenting program has reduced sexual violence and exploitation among adolescent girls in Tanzania by more than half, according to new research led by the University of Oxford's Department of Social Policy and Intervention. A separate study suggests the program could also deliver substantial savings to health services, offering a potentially affordable way to prevent violence against children.

mix_items.title: What families should know about postpartum psychosis
mix_items.summary: It's no wonder most people hadn't heard much about postpartum psychosis until it entered the news ecosystem in tragic fashion this year with the Lindsay Clancy case. Despite its severity, the illness isn't recognized as a standalone category in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)—the guidebook published by the American Psychiatric Association for classifying everything from anxiety and depression to obsessive-compulsive and trauma-related disorders.

mix_items.title: Deep-sea mollusk houses bacteria in tiny 'dragon balls,' revealing a new symbiotic structure
mix_items.summary: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have discovered a previously unknown specialized organelle structure in a deep-sea mollusk living at cold seeps in the South China Sea. Dedicated to maintaining bacterial symbiosis, this newly identified survival mechanism provides new insights into how deep-sea organisms adapt to nearly oxygen-free environments and opens new directions for research on chemosymbiosis, organelle evolution and deep-sea ecosystems.

mix_items.title: Urgent care emerges as a promising setting for imaging low back pain
mix_items.summary: Low back pain accounts for some of the highest health care spending in the U.S. Given how many patients are affected, even small changes in imaging practices could substantially impact health care resource use. A retrospective cohort study led by Mass General Brigham researchers found that only 24 of 2,924 urgent care lumbar spine X-rays for uncomplicated low back pain were followed by emergency department advanced imaging within 30 days.

mix_items.title: New method maps DNA folding and epigenetic marks in single cells
mix_items.summary: A new experimental procedure developed by researchers at Yale School of Medicine could help scientists better understand how DNA structure influences disease and development.

mix_items.title: When rain finally does come to drylands, only some microbes in the soil 'awaken'
mix_items.summary: In arid regions, the microbes that power threatened dryland soil ecosystems called biological soil crusts stay dormant over long periods, only "awakening" when they sense moisture from infrequent rainfall. Now, a team led by researchers at Penn State—driven by projections that those biocrusts will decline by as much as 40% in the next 45 years—found that when a dryland soil does get wet, most of the microbes in the biocrust stay inactive. It's a discovery that will inform ongoing efforts to conserve and restore biocrusts, according to the researchers.

mix_items.title: Biologists reveal chlorophyll-building enzyme's structure for first time and clarify its mechanism
mix_items.summary: Plants are green because of a pigment that is key to photosynthesis: chlorophyll. In its production, the enzyme chlorophyll synthase plays an important role. As part of an international collaboration, researchers from Osnabrück University, the Center Algatech in Třeboň and the University of Sheffield have now succeeded in deciphering the structure of this enzyme and gaining valuable insights into its mechanism. The findings are published in the journal Nature Chemical Biology.

mix_items.title: Psychedelic aftereffects may offer a window into psychotic symptoms
mix_items.summary: Every night, as he fell asleep, a 25-year-old man saw an eye in his ceiling. It was huge and unblinking, and it felt as if the whole world was being sucked into it. He didn't have psychosis, and he wasn't on drugs. But he had taken psychedelics in the past, and he was worried enough to contact Max Greenwald, an M.D.-Ph.D. student at Yale School of Medicine, with a question: Was he developing psychosis?

mix_items.title: Scientists challenge the dream of bringing extinct species back to life
mix_items.summary: Could extinction itself become a thing of the past? Advances in biotechnology, including ancient DNA sequencing, genome analysis and gene editing, have led some to believe that it may be possible to bring extinct species back to life.

mix_items.title: Chip identifies cells by their electrical signature, then separates them with a precisely aimed sound wave
mix_items.summary: In biomedicine, sorting cells accurately without damaging them remains a persistent problem. Current methods, like fluorescence-activated cell sorting, rely on labeling the cells extrinsically, which can stress the cells, alter their behavior and even interfere with the assay. A collaborative study between researchers in Singapore and China has now developed a noninvasive, label-free method to sort cells.

mix_items.title: Team discovers key pathway in heart lymphatic vessel development
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Children's Hospital Los Angeles have uncovered molecular signals that shape a little-understood network of vessels in the heart, offering new insight into both its normal formation and its response to injury.

mix_items.title: From remedy to prevention: Researchers call for proactive approach to protect the human right to water
mix_items.summary: More than 2 billion people, or approximately one-quarter of the world's population, lack access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene, according to the United Nations Children's Fund. Today, 16 years after the U.N. General Assembly recognized this access as a fundamental human right, its legal protection is well established, but the reality on the ground lags behind.

mix_items.title: Symbolic clay figurines change our understanding of the prehistoric Middle East
mix_items.summary: Newly discovered artifacts are evidence of the earliest known example of a tradition of making clay figurines in the Middle East—and challenge long-held beliefs about when and how clay began to be used for symbolic purposes in the region, according to a study published in PLOS One by Laurent Davin from The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Monkey foot and palm prints differ between individuals, as they do in humans
mix_items.summary: In three species of monkey, the complex pattern of ridges on the feet and palms varies between individuals, similar to human fingerprints, according to a study published in the open-access journal PLOS One by Juliana Vieira Flores Sales at Universidade de Brasília and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Misunderstandings about statistics common even among experienced researchers
mix_items.summary: Even researchers and people with extensive training in statistics often find it difficult to interpret statistical results correctly. This is shown by a new systematic review carried out by Uppsala University and others, in which researchers have analyzed 55 studies involving over 15,000 participants. The work is published in PLOS One.

mix_items.title: Spain's massive stone tombs reveal collective burials continued well into Bronze Age
mix_items.summary: Iberian people continued using, and possibly building, massive necropolises well into the Bronze Age, according to a study published in PLOS One by Eduardo Vijande-Vila of the University of Cádiz, Spain, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Jolting awake often associated with poorer sleep and higher anxiety, survey finds
mix_items.summary: People who frequently startle awake while falling asleep—a phenomenon researchers call "sleep starts" or hypnic jerks—report poorer sleep quality, greater insomnia severity and higher anxiety than those who do not, according to a new study published in PLOS Mental Health by Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus of Paris Lodron University Salzburg, Austria, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Children's recess activity in extreme heat highlights need for adult-guided safety measures
mix_items.summary: In a survey of 170 elementary students in the Phoenix, Arizona, metropolitan area over August–September 2024 (the average maximum temperature during this period was 97°F; 36.1°C), students reported feeling "a lot hot" directly after recess in 45% of surveys—and higher perceived heat was associated with greater physical activity intensity, according to a study published in PLOS Global Public Health by Kylie Wilson from the University of Arizona Cancer Center, United States, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Could your genes affect your medications? New study highlights high probability
mix_items.summary: Everyone in a diverse, nearly 100,000-person sample carried at least one genetic variant that affects how their body processes medications, and a quarter of those people had been prescribed a medication that is known to be impacted by the variant they carried, a new University of Pittsburgh–led analysis reveals in Science Translational Medicine.

mix_items.title: How gut antibodies protect against colon cancer
mix_items.summary: Antibodies that coat the lining of your gut may be playing an important role in preventing colon cancer from developing, Rockefeller University scientists have discovered.

mix_items.title: Excess reliance on AI could harm independent thinking in humanities education
mix_items.summary: The increasing use of content generated using artificial intelligence (AI) tools in university humanities classrooms is challenging what we think of as traditional academic integrity, intellectual responsibility and the authority of teachers, according to research in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development.

mix_items.title: Giving the voice a face: Virtual avatars may ease distress in schizophrenia
mix_items.summary: Patients with schizophrenia can come face to face in virtual reality with an avatar representing the voice they hear, which is often threatening or abusive. According to a study by researchers at Semmelweis University, published in Acta Psychologica, the treatment was associated with significant reductions in the frequency of the voices and the distress they caused, with more than 40% of participants showing meaningful improvement overall. While the results are promising, the researchers stress that VR-Avatar therapy cannot replace medication and should only be used as an add-on treatment.

mix_items.title: Ancient DNA reveals rare genetic condition behind a 1,600-year-old infant's single eye socket
mix_items.summary: Cyclopia is the most severe form of a rare birth condition in which the developing brain fails to divide into two separate halves. This can also affect facial development, sometimes leaving the baby with a single eye socket in the center of the forehead and severe facial abnormalities. Most babies born with this condition either die before or soon after birth. It is so rare that it occurs in roughly 1 in 100,000 births, so finding physical evidence of it from modern times is difficult, let alone from historical ones.

mix_items.title: Training AI to see cells in context improves detection in pathology images
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence can help identify cells in digital pathology images, but densely packed tissue remains a challenge: neighboring cells may be merged, counted twice or missed entirely. Researchers at Koç University have developed a training strategy that improves detection by teaching AI to consider how cells are arranged within the tissue.

mix_items.title: Youth and caregiver reports of mental health issues differ, but both perspectives needed
mix_items.summary: Psychiatric assessments of children and adolescents commonly incorporate reports from both youth and their caregivers. However, they may identify substantially different mental health problems, potentially influencing diagnosis, treatment planning and estimates of psychiatric disorder prevalence.

mix_items.title: Family activities, volunteering and exercise show links to greater psychological resilience, study finds
mix_items.summary: A research team led by the School of Public Health, LKS Faculty of Medicine of the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), recently conducted one of the largest and most systematic studies to date on predictors of psychological resilience. Analyzing data from 26,210 Hong Kong residents, the researchers systematically evaluated 208 candidate predictors and ultimately identified 35 factors associated with an individual's capacity to cope with adversity.

mix_items.title: New 'FITdb' database reveals the genetic drivers of immune cell function
mix_items.summary: Scientists at La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) have developed a critical hub for functional genomics and immune cell research. LJI Assistant Professor Miguel Reina-Campos directs the new Functional Immunogenomics and Transcriptomics database (FITdb), a freely accessible resource that brings together functional genomics datasets for immune cell investigations.

mix_items.title: New review of the first oral PCSK9 drug, a needle-free option for high cholesterol
mix_items.summary: A new review from Binghamton University School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Science explores how Lipfendra (enlicitide) can be beneficial for those who have intolerances to injectable medications. The review was recently published in Annals of Pharmacotherapy and was authored by clinical assistant professors Taylor Clark, Rachel Lucas and Mia Lussier, as well as assistant professor Azadeh Nasuhidehnavi.

mix_items.title: For your health—the large and growing benefits of being smoke-free
mix_items.summary: It's important to celebrate big accomplishments. And when it comes to our health, the drop in U.S. smoking rates over the last six decades is certainly one to cheer.

mix_items.title: Drug ads can influence AI treatment recommendations, study finds
mix_items.summary: As people increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for health information, a new study by researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai raises questions about what happens when commercial advertising appears alongside a clinical question. The findings were reported in the Nov. 11 online issue of The Lancet Digital Health.

mix_items.title: US companies apply to explore deep-sea mining in area bordering Pacific island states
mix_items.summary: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back. The applications are part of a broader move by U.S. companies to […]

mix_items.title: What do a bean and a flamingo have in common? Finding the unexpected in nature photos

mix_items.summary: Four years ago, elders from several different communities in Angola’s southeastern highlands approached environmental anthropologist Kerllen Costa, saying they’d noticed an influx of people from outside the highlands coming there to hunt for bushmeat without obtaining permission from local chiefs. mix_items.summary: A long-term camera trap study has uncovered a treasure trove of wildlife in the Annamite mountains, that run through Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
